subtopic: ISRAEL-INQUIRY AS TO CANCELLATION OF EXPORT PERMIT FOR JET AIRCRAFT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of ihe Opposition):
subtopic: ISRAEL-INQUIRY AS TO CANCELLATION OF EXPORT PERMIT FOR JET AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Can the minister tell the house whether or not the permit in connection with the export of 24 jets to Israel was cancelled? If so, was it at the request of the Israeli government? What were the circumstances in connection with refunds, if any, to be made by Canada in consequence of the fact that Israel is not now to accept delivery?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: ISRAEL-INQUIRY AS TO CANCELLATION OF EXPORT PERMIT FOR JET AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the export permit was suspended by the government of Canada for the reason that the situation in the area was too critical to warrant shipment of arms into that area to anyone.
The arrangement for the purchase of jet planes was made between Canadair and the government of Israel, and at the request of the government of Israel the contract was liquidated. I am not sure of the exact terms but, as I understand the situation, the Israelis

inquiries of the Ministry paid the out of pocket expenses of Canadair on these particular planes up to the time the settlement was made. The planes themselves were turned back to the R.C.A.F. under a contract for exactly the same type of plane that was current at the time. The expense to the Israeli government was not great in proportion to the size of the order.

subtopic: ISRAEL-INQUIRY AS TO CANCELLATION OF EXPORT PERMIT FOR JET AIRCRAFT
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. On what date was the export permit suspended? Was it made at anyone's request? Why did the government find it necessary to adopt this attitude after having granted the export permit in order to provide for the supply of jets to permit the defence of Israel? Why did the government change its attitude and when?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: ISRAEL-INQUIRY AS TO CANCELLATION OF EXPORT PERMIT FOR JET AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my memory is reasonably good but I cannot remember dates offhand.

subtopic: ISRAEL-INQUIRY AS TO CANCELLATION OF EXPORT PERMIT FOR JET AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Approximately?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: ISRAEL-INQUIRY AS TO CANCELLATION OF EXPORT PERMIT FOR JET AIRCRAFT
speechtext: I cannot say even approximately. The permit was suspended when Israel moved into Egypt on an aggressive expedition. The suspension of the export permit was action taken by the government of Canada. Perhaps I should say the suspension of the export permit was taken on the initiative of the government of Canada because one of the conditions on which the export permit was granted was that the planes would not be used except for defensive purposes and Israel at the time of the suspension was committing an act of aggression. The cancellation of the order for planes was made on the initiative of the government of Israel. As I say, the government of Canada was not a participant in that transaction; that is, it was not a participant in the sale of the planes to Israel.

subtopic: ISRAEL-INQUIRY AS TO CANCELLATION OF EXPORT PERMIT FOR JET AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Perhaps the minister
would allow me one further question. Did the Canadian government advise the government of Israel at the time it suspended this export permit that what was being done was because of what the minister described as an act of aggression on the part of Israel? How long after the Israeli forces moved forward was that suspension of the export permit taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: ISRAEL-INQUIRY AS TO CANCELLATION OF EXPORT PERMIT FOR JET AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I would have to have notice of these questions. I could give my friend actual dates by consulting the records but I do not remember these dates offhand.

subtopic: ISRAEL-INQUIRY AS TO CANCELLATION OF EXPORT PERMIT FOR JET AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Possibly the minister
could give further information tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: ISRAEL-INQUIRY AS TO CANCELLATION OF EXPORT PERMIT FOR JET AIRCRAFT
speechtext: Yes, I would be pleased to.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO EFFECT OF UNITED STATES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REFERENCE TO EFFECT OF UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Does the minister agree with the opinion expressed by Ezra Taft Benson, the United States secretary of agriculture, in a letter to the editor of the Vancouver Herald and reported by the Canadian Press in today's newspapers to the effect that the United States fire-sale wheat

export policies have not hurt other wheat exporting countries including Canada, and has not affected sales abroad?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: REFERENCE TO EFFECT OF UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to say that this time I have read the Globe and Mail, which I think is the newspaper to which my hon. friend referred. Someone put a copy into my hands as I was coming downstairs to the house. I read the remarks of secretary Benson and I do not agree with them. I think that if Mr. Benson will consult his officers they will explain to him the views of the Canadian government in some detail because the views of the Canadian government have been explained to his officers through our continuing committee.
I noticed one other statement in the report. Although the government of the United States has reduced wheat acreage, the governments of other exporting countries have not reduced wheat acreage. If Mr. Benson will consult the acreage figures for Canada he will find that the acreage planted to wheat in this country has dropped from about 28 million acres at the end of the second world war to a little less than 20 million acres today.

subtopic: REFERENCE TO EFFECT OF UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a supplementary question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce arising out of a statement he made a short while ago in the chamber to the effect that Canadian producers have reduced their wheat acreage. speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: REPORTED SALES BY UNITED STATES TO JAPAN
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, we have enjoyed a market for high grade wheat in Japan for several years. speechtext:
May I
ask a question of the Minister of Finance. Has the minister seen the report in Maclean's Building Reports that the volume of construction in Canada during January was down by 42 per cent as compared with January, 1956? Does the minister think a decline of these proportions in any way satisfies the declared objectives of the Bank of Canada, and is the government giving consideration to what should be done in the face of such a decline in building construction?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPORTED EFFECT OF CREDIT RESTRICTIONS ON CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Yes, I have seen the report, Mr. Speaker, and the consideration which is being given to the problem of controlling inflation, while not stopping the desired growth of the country, goes on every day. The accumulation of evidence such as this with regard to the effects of a policy of restraint is welcome. At the same time, the minister and the government recognize that one cannot carry a policy of restraint to a point where it operates in a manner which one would not like and the most difficult decision that can be made will be made as to when the policy of restraint can be eased in order that the present excellent good times in Canada may be continued.
Inquiries of the Ministry

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. From the questions directed to him in connection with the budget, would the minister get the impression the official opposition is very anxious to have an early election?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF EARLY PRESENTATION
speechtext: I should also like to refer to some words which the Minister of Finance used which have been puzzling me a bit. I think he said that preparations on the budget were hardly yet under way. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF EARLY PRESENTATION
speechtext: I do not think I need go into the details as to how long and how much work is involved in preparing a budget. This process has not been completed as yet, and that is what I had in mind when I said that the work had not begun. I was referring to myself, of course. subtopic: BORDEN, P.E.I.-CAPE JOURIMAIN, N.B.  STATEMENT ON PROPOSED CAUSEWAY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Roberi H. Winters (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: BORDEN, P.E.I.-CAPE JOURIMAIN, N.B.  STATEMENT ON PROPOSED CAUSEWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to answer a question asked yesterday by the Liberal member for Queens (Mr. Matheson) about the work being done on the proposed causeway between Borden, Prince Edward Island, and Cape Tormentine, New Brunswick.

The situation is that the government of Prince Edward Island last year requested us to study the feasibility of a proposal to build a causeway from Prince Edward Island to New Brunswick, and we have done some work to that end.
This would be a project of major proportions. In estimating its cost an important factor will be the source of supply of suitable rock. The province specifically requested assistance in determining the possibility of obtaining suitable rock from the Cape Tormentine area.
On the basis of geological reports, test holes were drilled and samples sent to our testing laboratory in Ottawa. These cores have been undergoing tests but a full evaluation is not yet complete.
Concurrent with the laboratory testing, a field performance test has been established adjacent to the Canadian National Railways' dock at Cape Tormentine in which samples of the best stone obtained from the Tormentine drilling, as well as other local quarry material, are under observation. These tests were started last fall and will continue until the samples have been subjected to a full year's cycle of weather and sea conditions. The results of the field test will be a further check on the laboratory tests which are being reviewed at the present time.
In addition to the technical study, we are making a full financial and economic analysis. In this we have had the guidance of observations made in the preliminary report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. This study will include a forecast of the over-all economic benefits from a causeway as against the type of service now provided with the ferries. Arrangements are being made to have this financial and economic study carried out by the accounting and management consultant firm of Price, Waterhouse and Company with whom we have already had discussion.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Prime Minister. Does the government intend to deliver the Alberta Indian Association petition to the Queen to its proper destination while the responsible hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) is cavorting in Newfoundland, or is this petition to be interred in the tombs of Ottawa files and mark another retrogade step in Canadian democracy?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian democracy has reached the stage when the provision in the Act of Settlement is no longer appropriate in respect of some kinds of petitions. I have not seen this petition. The usual practice, when a petition is sent to Government House, is for the staff to transfer it to the minister most directly concerned with the subject matter. It is done in that way because under the constitutional system the governor general now does not act without the advice of his ministers.
If the matter is one that can involve no doubt the minister may himself tender such advice as he feels certain would have the approval of all his colleagues because, in tendering the advice, he engages the solidarity of all of his colleagues, and when there is any doubt as to whether that would be objected to by any of his colleagues the matter is brought to their attention in a meeting of cabinet for a decision as to what advice should be given.
Now, I have not seen this petition. I am under the impression that it is a petition founded upon the assertion that is being made many times by representatives of the original inhabitants of this part of the North American continent, that they are not subject to Canadian laws but they are allies of Canada. Well, now, a petition that would be based upon that foundation would not be submitted to Her Majesty with any recommendation that it should be recognized because the position that is taken by the government is that all the inhabitants of Canada are subject to Canadian law.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there is one particular point I should like to deal with arising out of something the Prime Minister said yesterday which I think should be clarified. First of all may I say that as the committee is aware this group is in full support of this legislation. We hope it will not be long until the bill is passed and it will be possible for the government to implement it.
However, something happened yesterday which puzzled me. The Prime Minister knows that for a number of years I have tried to persuade the house, thus far in vain, to accept an amendment to the Income Tax Act with particular reference to the section of the act which prescribes secrecy so far as information obtained under the act is concerned. Every time I have introduced that amendment the Minister of National Revenue has endeavoured to make a strong case against' it by asserting vehemently that secrecy regarding information obtained under the Income Tax Act must prevail. I find that the provision in the Income Tax Act which has been quoted to me by the Minister of National Revenue is also contained in the Dominion Succession Duty Act, section 55 of which reads as follows:
(1)	No person employed in the service of Her Majesty shall communicate or allow to be communicated to any person not legally entitled thereto, any information obtained under the provisions of this act, or allow any such person to inspect or have access to any written statement furnished under the provisions of this act.
(2)	Any persons violating any of the provisions of this section are liable on summary conviction to a penalty not exceeding two hundred dollars.
I raise the question whether the Prime Minister did not violate that section of the act yesterday when he told us in considerable detail about two estates which he named as the Killam estate and the Sir James Dunn estate. He indicated the windfalls that had been obtained from those two estates. The Prime Minister then related those windfalls to the $100 million involved in this resolution, and went on to say that something over $50 million had been paid in from one of those estates.

I do not object to our getting this information. As a matter of fact I have been trying to get the income tax legislation amended so we could get this type of information. But on other occasions when we have asked for information in the hands of cabinet ministers, obtained by them under the provisions of the income tax legislation, we have been told every time that because of the secrecy provisions we could not be given the information. How does the Prime Minister explain the fact that yesterday in face of section 55 (1) and (2) of the Dominion Succession Duty Act he gave out information about the succession duties paid by these two estates?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps the hon. gentleman will find that technically I violated the statute, but I did not think I was doing that. I was simply repeating information which had been published pretty generally in the newspapers since the deaths of these two wealthy Canadians. I was not giving precise figures and I had not obtained precise figures. I was giving approximate figures which were known to the public and I am sure to every hon. member of the house. It was general knowledge that there had been unusually large payments in respect to succession duties.
Perhaps I should not have given any figure at all, perhaps I should have been content with saying that there were unusually large payments in respect of succession duties. I hope it will not cause inconvenience to anyone and I do not think it will. As the Leader of the Opposition said, it was not necessary to put any names on the record as everyone knew who those two wealthy Canadians were who had died in the period referred to.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the preliminary discussion of this resolution I was impressed with the emphasis the Prime Minister placed upon the importance of a teacher training program. Most of our teacher training programs are carried out in the smaller colleges, particularly the liberal arts colleges who concern themselves mainly with the humanities. I am wondering whether there is to be some specific regulation or some specific mention in the bill which will assure these smaller liberal arts colleges the consideration that is required under this new legislation.
The tendency is toward centralization, in education as in many other fields, and in every case these private endowments go to the larger centres of learning. Sir, the very nature of the work of the Canada Council, concerned as it will be with the humanities
Canada Council
and the liberal arts and sciences, would suggest that in a special way the smaller institutions devoted to this kind of activity will be taken care of.
I wonder if the Prime Minister would care to comment on how this may be managed by way of regulation or legislation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: There will be no provision for the Governor in Council to make regulations concerning the way in which members of the council should discharge their responsibilities. I think the matter which the hon. gentleman has in mind will be taken care of because of its real merits in the light of the objectives which it will be the duty of the Canada Council to pursue.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: I take it from the Prime Minister's comment that the Canada Council committee, then, will have complete responsibility for allocating both these funds; it will be a matter entirely within their jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Within the limits fixed by the statute. The capital grants fund can be allocated in a province only in proportion to the population of that province, though the allocation to the ten provinces need not be made in the same year or years. This is intended to be a provision for ten years, and it will be provided in the bill that the sum available will be divided in proportion to the population of the province; but there will be no requirement that each province should get its share at the same time. There will also be a requirement that the scheme which will receive part of the allocation of the grant attributed to a province shall be one that will appear to the Canada Council as worthy of encouragement; and it will be only a matching grant, that is to say, an amount equal to what will be provided by the institution itself from some other source.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to comment briefly on the resolution before the discussion on this phase of the measure is terminated, and I want in particular to say what has been in my mind concerning the discussion which has taken place thus far, and whether or not the reservation which I made on January 18 will be continued.
I said at that time, when I spoke on this resolution, that I would have to reserve my judgment with regard to the Canada Council until I had given it much further consideration. In my mind particularly, at that time, was the question of priority; I wanted to find out whether or not the government intended, this session, to make any improvement in old age pension benefits and in certain other social security benefits. I said I thought that

Canada Council
this question was largely a matter of priorities. Whether I would support the setting up of the Canada Council now would depend on whether the government was, first of all, prepared to take care of these other matters which I believe to be of more importance to the people of Canada-to far more people than could ever receive benefits by reason of the Canada Council.
I have not changed my mind, because I have been able to obtain from the government no satisfaction in answer to the questions I have asked and to questions asked by other hon. members. There has been no indication whatsoever that the government intends to proceed this session to grant increased benefits to the needy people of this country, and because of that fact I still feel, Mr. Chairman, that we should not proceed with the setting up of this Canada Council until such time as those other important priorities have been attended to.
I still oppose going ahead with this scheme, and putting up $100 million of the taxpayers' money for the purposes envisaged in this resolution. I cannot feel we are doing the right thing by the people of Canada by denying them an increase in old age pension benefits, and war veterans allowance benefits in view of the fact that these benefits are now so far below the level which we had hoped would be maintained over the years. Today, as the Prime Minister knows and as his colleagues must know, the $40 a month received by an old age pensioner will buy no more than about $20 worth of goods and services; a pensioner is no better off today, with his $40, than he was with the $20 he was receiving before we made the increase.
I said in this house on January 18, and I repeat it, that before we go into this area of "frills"-and that is what this is-a frill -we ought to be taking care of some of the things which are more important to our people. But I have failed, thus far, to get any satisfaction from the government, and since I have had no reassurance on this subject I must say, now, that I am strongly opposed to the passing of this resolution and of the bill which will be brought in and dependent upon it.
I want also to say, Mr. Chairman, that I have to maintain my opposition with regard to the need for this proposal. There is no need to have a Canada Council for the purpose of distributing university grants or giving aid to universities. We have been able, in the past, to extend help to the universities of this country without a Canada Council, and we can continue to do it on an extended scale. There is no necessity for having a Canada Council in order to distribute scholarships. That has been done quite well, in the 
past, with the machinery we had; the whole difficulty lay in the amount of money which was being distributed in the form of scholarships and aid to students in improving their educational standards. I maintain that all we need do today is use the agencies which now exist, and see to it that the provincial rights are recognized and maintained. We can do that by making available any moneys that we feel we have for this purpose to university organizations themselves, to the departments of education in the various provinces and, possibly, to other existing agencies. While I am in entire sympathy with the idea of extending grants to the universities for capital and other purposes, and making available scholarships on a wider scale than in the past to worthy students, I cannot feel it is necessary to set up the Canada Council in order to do this.
So far as culture is concerned, Mr. Chairman, I must also maintain the position I took when I spoke earlier on this matter. You just cannot buy culture; you cannot substitute a "canned" culture for the real stuff that develops spontaneously out of the experience of the people, their hopes and the memories that come from their own hearts; and if any attempt is made to impose a culture of an artificial, "canned" type on the Canadian people I will resist it with all my strength. I say at the same time that it is wise for us to try to encourage the development of every phase of culture that we possibly can but I still maintain that you cannot overlook the fact that before you start on such a project you have got to take care of the actual needs of the people. I maintain that the greatest priority in Canada today is to take care of those people who are forced to live below the borderline of poverty. That is the reason I am taking the position I take today.
I am not saying that at some time in the future, if the government has looked after these other matters and if we have the money to spend, whether it be from windfalls or any other source, we would oppose the establishment of a Canada Council provided we knew fully what its purposes were and provided we knew that its objectives were sound and good. I am not saying that at all. But let the government first give us these other assurances and then we may agree with their desire to set up a council.
I should like to add a word in passing about one phase which I think was most unfortunate and about which I do not think the Prime Minister feels too happy having regard to the interpretation that the newspapers have put on it. I hold in my hand today's Montreal Gazette, and on the front page there is this heading: "P.M. Staggers

Commons-Dunn, Killam Estates Finance Culture." I did not place that interpretation on what he said but I do think it was unfortunate it was mentioned and I am wondering how many Liberals are going to go throughout the country in the election campaign and say to the people: "Now, do not worry about the Canada Council and the $100 million it is going to cost because the money is not coming out of taxation. Actually what has happened is that two great big estates have supplied the $100 million and it will not come out of the taxpayers at all." That is utter foolishness and if any of that sort of thing is done, believe me it is going to be exposed with all of the energy that we can command. I am just as sure as I stand here that that will be done in the campaign by some campaigners. I am not saying it will be done by the Prime Minister. I am not accusing him at all.
But let me point out this important thing. I think it is a dangerous precedent at any time to say that you have received a windfall from the estates of certain men who have died and therefore you feel that you have enough money to be able to do something in which these people were interested. They said they were interested in making bequests to certain things such as the development of culure in Canada and because they said so you say that you are sort of influenced to go ahead now that you have their money.
There is no more justification for taking that position than there would be if I were to direct that a thousand dollars which I may pay in income tax this year should be earmarked for the development of an athletic council in Canada to encourage participation in athletics. There is no more justification in the one case than in the- other. I do not feel I have any right whatsoever to direct the government how it shall spend the taxes it takes from me except through consideration of the general estimates in the house. I do have that right but with respect to directing that a part of what I contribute in the form of taxation shall be used for this or that purpose I say that should not have any relation' whatsoever to anything the government has in its mind as a desirable thing to do.
I wanted to mention that because in the forthcoming election campaign I do not want to hear any Liberals going across the country and saying to the people: "Do not worry about this at all because you do not have to pay for it. The money is coming out of Killam and Sir James Dunn, who are dead." I am issuing a warning because I know what has happened in campaigns before. I have 82715-65
Canada Council
been through them and that sort of thing happens all too frequently.
I want to make it abundantly clear that we oppose the passing of the resolution. If there is some satisfactory explanation of what the government is going to do with regard to social security measures when the bill is before us, we may change our minds at that time.
Let me utter one other word of warning.
I want to repeat what I said before. The government should be mighty careful about who constitute the personnel of the Canada Council and I shall not rest easy until I know who they are.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: There will be some Grits.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question. When the Canada Council is set up will it be on the same basis with respect to receiving gifts as our charitable organizations? If an amount is given as a gift to the Canada Council or is left by way of a bequest in a will, will that amount be treated in the same way as charitable gifts are treated at the present time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will find when the bill is introduced that there is a clause making that provision.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall only be a minute. It seemed to me that the hon. member for Peace River covered everything except naming the Council the Killam-Dunn succession duty arts council. I do not think we should censure the Prime Minister for informing us of the method to be used in setting up the council. He was very forthright in telling us how the money is to be obtained. I am a little surprised at the method to be used because I inquired of him yesterday whether this might create a precedent. He indicates that he does not think so but I am wondering what method will be used in the future to take care of the deficits which I am sure will arise from time to time. Are we going to finance the council by waiting for more windfalls, if you want to use that expression, and making additions to capital account or will it be the government's intention to vote the sums required from time to time to make up deficits in the interest account?
It seems to me that is a fairly important question because as the matter stands now and having in mind the amount of money involved there may be many millions of people who have some claim on the bounty here with respect to the funds that are being used. They may be people who can say very rightly that they are not going to obtain any particular direct benefit although it may be

Canada Council
said that the country generally is farther ahead. I think that those people would expect that all that would be necessary would be a grant on an annual or some other type of basis to meet immediate needs. They can honestly say that the money in this case has come from the effort of many people possibly over several generations and why is it necessary that the whole endowment should be paid out of the funds of the 1957 fiscal year?
I therefore ask the Prime Minister if he has considered the possibility of financing the council on a year to year basis or some basis of that kind and whether he sees it as always being necessary to contribute capital amounts from which interest will be drawn to make up any deficit? If that should be the case, it seems to me that each year the taxpayer is contributing a lump sum which will be used over many years. As the hon. member for Peace River has said, there are people who will question the fact that, while they are on a fixed income at the moment such as old age pensions, veterans allowances and blind pensions, this amount should be set aside all in one year.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Last night I had the privilege of addressing a gathering in Ottawa in company with three of my colleagues from this house, one from each of the other parties. On that occasion the representative of the Social Credit party presented to the audience the principles upon which his party is founded. They were all extremely high minded aspirations towards civic virtue, and I felt impelled at the end of them to remark that about all I had been able to gather of the policies of Social Credit was that they were "agin sin". This afternoon, though, I find I have to amend that because I have read the speech delivered last night by the hon. member for Macleod and listened to the leader of that group this afternoon, and I discover they are "agin culture", and I suspect for the same reason, that both sin and culture have the habit of expanding human experience to a degree that would be alarming to those who find their best fishing in the muddy waters of ignorance.
I was very interested also this afternoon in the remarks of the leader of the Social Credit group who based their objection to the Canada Council on the ground that the government has not seen fit to raise old age pensions. I am at one with them in deploring the fact the government has not seen fit to reveal its plans, if it has any, in this regard. But I would be much more impressed with the sincerity of my Social Credit colleagues if I had heard them, on any occasion, 
voicing the objections that have come from this group to the manner in which oil companies and oil pipeline companies mulct the general public of this country of the tribute they draw from their operations. There has been not a word from these people. The oil pipeline companies can work little stock market rackets robbing the general public and reducing the possible revenues that might be devoted to the raising of old age pensions, but not a word comes from our Social Credit friends. I suspect, Mr. Chairman, that it is a genuine revulsion against thought and culture that really moves them in this instance, and they have been able to find what they think is going to be a very useful political peg upon which to hang that genuine revulsion against knowledge and culture.
I noted in reading over the report from the United Kingdom the actions that our friends in Britain have taken with regard to an activity similar to that projected for the Canada Council.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Work it out on a per capita basis.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Oh yes, we will work it out on a per capita basis if you wish, although that will tell you nothing. What we can tell you is that hard pressed people such as the people of Britain, who have suffered in a way that no other people have suffered-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Well, they are centuries old.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Yes, they are centuries old, but they have suffered bitter losses in two major wars and a major depression, yet they are prepared to go ahead with this project on a more generous scale

than we are. The reason, Mr. Chairman, I suggest is that they have a better concept of the purpose of human life than is prevalent on the North American continent.
I have noted some of the comments in this house with regard to what is called culture.
I have noticed, for instance, comments from our Social Credit friends that we should not expect the state to endow these things. I recall that the hon. member for Peace River, on January 18, cited as an example of the fine, sturdy, individual enterprise that leads to success in the arts, the career of Mr. Raymond Massey. He suggested that Mr. Massey, this outstanding Canadian actor, had reached that point without having to be subsidized. I wonder what the prairie wheat farmers, who subsidized Mr. Raymond Massey in his climb to the top of the theatrical ladder, would say to that? What nonsense! Mr. Massey was subsidized, and subsidized from the pockets of the Canadian people, in a manner in which apparently some members of this house wish to avoid in the future.
We hear some rather pathetic statements in this chamber, and they do not all come from the Social Credit party. There was some criticism the other day of a certain C.B.C. program. I was rather interested in that criticism, interested in that fine outburst of hairy-chestedness in opposing a certain program of ballet. X did not see it myself. Right at the start I shall say I think I would have found 90 minutes of "Swan Lake" on T.V. a little hard to take. In the first place, I doubt whether T.V. is a suitable medium for ballet. In the second place, I am not particularly fond of the "Swan Lake" ballet. What struck me as pathetic was that this gentleman was opposing it on the assumption that he did not like ballet. The pathetic part of it is that he did not know whether or not he liked ballet because all he had seen was this particular example of a particular style of classical ballet.
If he were in the house this afternoon, I would suggest to him that there are examples of ballet that I believe would appeal equally to his earthy temperament as they do to mine. For instance, if he had been looking at Offenbach's "Gaiete Parisienne", he would have regretted very much if, for the gracefully waving legs of the ladies in the can can, there had suddenly been substituted the squirmings and writhings of the wrestlers about whom he was so anxious. He might even have gained the considerable pleasure from viewing Agnes de Mille's "Rodeo", where the ballet dancers use a western motif and exhibit a skill and physical control that is far beyond the capacities of any of those overweight phonies who writhe and groan 82715-65i
Canada Council
on the mats. As I say, I think it is pathetic that people reject a human experience from ignorance.
I believe the government is to be commended that they are taking one very slight step towards broadening the horizons of the Canadian people. I was rather struck with the suggestion of the leader of the Social Credit party that only a few people are going to benefit from the Canada Council. If I thought that for one minute, I would vote against it. The whole purpose of it is to create a climate of thought and knowledge in Canada that will enrich the lives of the people of Canada.
Surely that is the purpose of it, and surely that is a worthy purpose. My great regret is that we are devoting such a small sum of money in comparison with the sums we devote to other aspects of our society.
I want to conclude, Mr. Chairman, by suggesting that it is shameful hypocrisy to pretend that there is a valid reason for voting against this measure because the government has not as yet increased old age pensions, family allowances or any of the other social services which they ought to be increasing and which they would be well able to increase if they were following fiscal policies, which would be opposed by our friends of the Social Credit party, but fiscal policies nevertheless that would be designed to bring to the public treasury a very much larger share of the wealth produced by the people of this country.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the Prime Minister introduced the resolution on January 18 he had this to say, as reported at page 397 of Hansard:
We shall also be asking parliament to provide from the consolidated revenue sum a further sum of $50 million to be known as "the university capital grants fund" to be distributed by the council as a contribution toward the financing of specific building projects of which it may approve in the furthering of its general objectives-
The general objectives, of course, Mr. Chairman, are the furthering of the arts, the social sciences and the humanities. I continue with the quotation:
-to the extent of not more than 50 per cent in any one case, the contributions to be expended over a period of years-not necessarily in equal instalments of an equal fraction each year but by apportionment generally, to the institutions of the various provinces in proportion to their population.
A little farther down on the same page the Prime Minister said:
The federal government does not feel that it should be the sole patron of the arts, the humanities and the social sciences or the only source of capital for the universities.
From listening to the Prime Minister speak I got the definite impression that those

Canada Council
moneys were to be apportioned entirely for the furthering of studies in the arts, the humanities and the social sciences, but to make absolutely sure that was so I asked the Prime Minister a question the following Monday. At page 436 of Hansard I asked him the following question:

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Does the government intend to assist the universities in providing the greatly enlarged training facilities that will be needed to train the greatly increased numbers of scientists, engineers, doctors and dentists, of which this country is so critically short today, so that we may avoid a continuance of that shortage?
It was a perfectly honest, normal question, asking for information regarding the spending of this money. The Prime Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, the government's intentions so far as they have been crystalized in decisions have already been announced to the house, and that procedure will be followed when other decisions are reached.
That is no answer at all. I continued:

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Was not the government's decision in this regard announced on Friday by the Prime Minister when he announced there would be no assistance given to the universities except to provide extra training facilities for the arts and humanities?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
If my hon. friend is of the opinion that he was given on Friday the answer to the question put this morning, I cannot see why he repeats it.
I cannot see why he refused to answer my question. I was still after information, and I said:
In reply to the Prime Minister's answer may I say this. It was my impression that he said that no extra facilities would be provided except for the humanities. I am trying to clear up the question as to the sciences and engineering.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
I hope my hon.
friend will not lose too much sleep over his wrong impression.
In other words the impression that money would not be provided for the training of people in engineering, the sciences, medicine and dentistry was completely wrong, according to the Prime Minister on that day. Yesterday, Mr. Chairman, in answer to a similar question, the Prime Minister had this to say, as reported at page 984 of Hansard:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution is not intended to provide for the establishment of increased facilities for a greatly increased number of students in engineering, medicine, dentistry and sciences.
In other words, a week ago Monday the Prime Minister in answer to a perfectly simple question asking for information, told me that I was completely wrong in assuming that no money would be made available for training in the sciences, engineering, dentistry and medicine. A week later, he told me exactly the reverse. The reason I bring this up, Mr. Chairman, is that this is one more example, as I see it, of what

appears to be a deliberate attempt by a senior minister to mislead the house. One day he told me one thing, and the next day he told me I was foolish for having such an idea in my head.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Thank heavens the seals at last came alive. Then a week later, when he was explaining the resolution, he said that what I had assumed, and what he said I was completely wrong about, was correct. I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether he would be good enough to explain why he gave me a completely misleading answer one day, and a week later said completely the opposite?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: I gave no misleading answer to the hon. gentleman here. On Friday, January 18, we were discussing this resolution. It is not the practice on the orders of the day and, in my opinion, should not be the practice, to refer to debates in process on a day when that debate is not taking place.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister not believe that a member has the right to rise in his place before the orders of the day are called and ask the Prime Minister, or any other minister, a question to clarify something which appeared to him reasonably clear, but on which he wanted to get specific information, on a most important point? Does the Prime Minister not think that a member has the right to rise and ask for clarification of an answer?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
Order. I think the hon. member is forgetting the fact that we are dealing with one specific resolution at this time. We are not dealing with questions asked or answers given on the orders of the day. If the hon. member would direct his discussion, or his questions, to the exact resolution under discussion it would be within our rules.
We must remember that in committee we are governed by strict relevancy to the item under consideration, and I do ask the cooperation of the hon. member in directing his questions to this resolution which, after all though it is somewhat broad in scope, is directed to certain purposes to which we should direct our attention.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my point is, did or did not the Prime Minister make two directly contradictory statements about the matter that is immediately under discussion in this committee? I claim he did.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
My answer is that I claim just as vigorously as the hon. gentleman claims the opposite that I did not

make two different statements. When I was discussing this resolution I was discussing its effect. The hon. gentleman was putting his question in general terms as to whether or not there would be anything done in respect of something that was not included in this resolution; and something is being done, and it will continue to be done, for our scientific investigation and aid to scientific investigation, for years. The national research council has been making increasingly large contributions and will continue to do so; but the hon. gentleman is not going to have me give answers to questions put in broad terms which will enable him then to say that I have been deliberately misleading the house.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was not referring in my question to what the research council is doing. I specifically said in my question, is there going to be any assistance given to the council with respect to specific studies, and the Prime Minister said I was completely wrong in assuming that it would not. Then a week later he said exactly that. These are two completely contradictory statements.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: Read it again.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext: I have one question I should like to ask the Prime Minister, because it is one point in which I am particularly interested and particularly cautious about. Can the Prime Minister tell us whether the intention of the Canada Council will be to publish literature and have the literature distributed to educational institutions such as public schools, high schools, universities or any other interested groups of an educational character?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PROVISION FOR ENCOURAGEMENT OF THE ARTS, HUMANITIES AND SOCIAL SCIENCES
speechtext:
I cannot say what might be done. I had not envisaged the Canada Council becoming a publishing house for desirable publications that might be distributed to schools. I would not be prepared to say that under the terms of the statute they would be precluded from doing something of that kind. The terms of the statute do not expressly provide that that may be done and I would be surprised if the council undertook to enter that field, though there might be some grants made to a university that had a university press, for example, to provide for the publication of something that would be looked upon as a matter of real value in promoting the study and enjoyment of the humanities, the social sciences or the arts. speechtext: If the experienced investment men came to the conclusion that the best possible investment was in government of Canada bonds I would be quite surprised, because I know of many good investments which may not have the immediate liquidity of Canadian government bonds but which have provided not only a good income but a substantial enhancement in capital value. Mr. Chairman, does not the Prime Minister see a certain inherent danger in such a procedure? program of expenditure for scholarships and other things, a program which will have hundreds or perhaps thousands of young people depending on revenue from this committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND EXPIRY DATE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, February 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 9, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. G. J. Hahn (New Westminster):
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND EXPIRY DATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the house for the kindness they showed me last Friday evening when they allowed me to call it six o'clock.
I rise in this debate at this time because of certain statements made by farm union organizations, and statements carried in the press such as the following: "A drop of 30 to 33 per cent in local poultry prices has occurred twice during the 1956 period as a result of eggs imported from the prairies or other areas into British Columbia". One might ask, what has that to do with the wheat board? The wheat board, Mr. Speaker, regulates the sale of feed grain outside the provinces and, as I understand it, the very fact that the wheat board has been set up by parliament and has regulatory power with regard to the selling of this grain does have a material effect on the cost of production of poultry, livestock, dairy and other farm products in British Columbia.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I understand that the main purpose behind this bill is to extend the life of the present wheat board act for another five years. I am quite satisfied, from present indications, that the hon. members of this house will support this particular bill.
We in British Columbia, particularly, realize the value of orderly marketing; we have other marketing boards in my province, and for a long time we have recognized the value not only of the wheat board but of other marketing agencies. However, I wonder whether the minister would be in a position later to advise the house as to the effect the wheat board, as now constituted, exerts upon activities which are dependent upon the grain


that goes through the hands of the board. I am talking of grain which goes into areas such as Ontario or British Columbia.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that before one decides to continue an act of this kind-an act which has been in operation now for a good number of years, working efficiently for at least one part of the country-we should be in a position to know exactly how it is operating in so far as the rest of the country is concerned. We should know what it does in the way of injuring, on the one hand, or of increasing and enhancing, on the other hand, productivity in other areas of the country. The prairie region is not the only one that is affected by this bill or by the implications of the act as it has been operated.
As I understand it, the operations of the act apply more directly to the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Grain farmers in those areas-and the minister may correct me later if I am wrong-are permitted to sell grain to other farmers within their own particular region without participation by the wheat board, but when other producers in other provinces require grain it would normally come through the wheat board under the terms of the act. They are permitted to sell grain for feed freely as long as it does not leave the province. However, when the grain leaves the province it is apparently a completely different matter.
Now, I ask the Minister of Finance, who took the estimates of the Minister of Agriculture through the house recently, a question with respect to that. I was interested in discovering whether the wheat board act applied in the case of grain grown in the Dawson Creek area, which I believe comes under wheat board regulations, and is hauled by rail by way of Edmonton to Vancouver. The minister was not sure whether or not that wheat would be subject to the wheat board regulations. He indicated at that time that he felt it would not be, because the grain is actually grown in the same province and is taken from the Dawson Creek area to Vancouver. If such is the case I would be pleased to hear the minister either substantiate or refute that statement because the Minister of Finance said he was not absolutely sure.
Common sense tells me that it would be perfectly legitimate and right to do so. The purpose in asking the question was to discover whether such grain carried from the Dawson Creek area through the province of Alberta and then into British Columbia would be eligible for the freight rate subsidy. Personally I see very little difference between paying the subsidy on such feed grain carried by rail and letting a trucker carry it from Dawson Creek to Vancouver and paying him

a subsidy lor doing so, thus reducing the cost of feed grain to the people of the lower mainland of British Columbia. That is certainly one question that causes us a great deal of concern.
During the course of the present session of parliament the procedure followed on the prairies for some time, whereby farmers within one province will sell feed grain to feed lots, poultry producers, dairy producers or neighbouring farmers at $18 to $20 a ton, has been drawn to the attention of the government. We on the lower mainland of the province of British Columbia have to pay $70 to $75 a ton for the same grain, and in some instances it is not nearly as good in quality.
I am particularly interested, as are the people of the lower mainland of British Columbia, in the effect of this policy. Here we have the development of poultry and dairy production on the prairies because the feed lot operators find they can get grain at a much lower price than we can in the lower mainland of British Columbia. The result has been that many of our producers have gone out of business. What effect does the operation of this act have on the farmers in the lower reaches of British Columbia?
The minister may dispute what I say about our farmers going out of business, but let me put the matter this way. In the last five years there has been a 20 per cent increase in the population of British Columbia, and under normal circumstances when the population increases industry within the area pretty well keeps pace. We did have a poultry industry and we still have a portion of it left. We did have a dairy industry and we still have a fairly good dairy industry. As far as hogs are concerned, I do not think we have a hog industry any more. Nevertheless, with the increase in our population we should have increased consumption of feed grains in the province.
To be more specific, I received a report from the feeds administration of the Department of Agriculture dated December 31, 1956. On pages 11 to 16 of that report there is a very clear indication of the situation with respect to the consumption of primary products in the province. For instance, in 1941- I realize I am going quite far back to show the picture-we purchased 9,519 tons of wheat, and from then on there was a substantial increase until the year 1947. In that year we purchased 131,964 tons of feed wheat. But each year since then there has been a progressive decrease in the amount of wheat purchased for feed purposes, until in 1956 we purchased only 65,830 tons of feed wheat.
Canadian Wheat Board Act In other words we purchased 131,964 tons in 1947, while we purchased only 65,830 tons in 1956.
The same thing is true of oats and barley. Taking the over-all totals, in 1941 we purchased 21,000 tons of grain and that figure rose to a total of better than 329,000 in 1947. Then it dropped to 162,381 tons in 1956, about half of what we purchased in 1947. I am sure it is very obvious that either one of two reasons is responsible for our using less feed grain in British Columbia. Either we are growing more in the lower mainland of British Columbia or in the Okanagan, or we have cut down on the production of dairy, poultry and other animals which consume this type of feed.
If the minister were to discuss this question with the Minister of Agriculture I am sure he would discover that what I have said is true, that since 1951 our population has increased by 20 per cent; yet over the past 10 years our purchases of grain to feed our poultry and livestock have fallen to less than half what they were. In my opinion we have a very difficult position, in that within the prairie provinces there is a marketing board which promotes the sale of feed grain to neighbouring farmers, poultry producers and others, with the result that these people have gone into poultry and livestock businesses in large measure.
I pose this question. What will be the effect on the economy of the country if the prairie grain producer finds himself in the position in which the Minister of Agriculture indicated he may possibly find himself in the very near future? You may ask me what statement I am referring to.
The statement was to the effect that all the prairie farmer needs is a year or two of bad or poor crops and he will not have any wheat to sell. As I see it, if the prairie farmer finds himself with a short crop he is going to have ready cash, cash which he would normally get by selling his wheat at these fire-sale prices of $18 to $20 a ton. If he has ready cash he is not going to sell that grain to his neighbouring farmer, the poultry producer or the feed lot in his area for $18 to $20 a ton; he is going to want $70 to $75 a ton.
In the meantime we in British Columbia have got rid of our record of performance chickens; we have got rid of our purebred stock, and since you cannot grow breeding stock overnight we are not going to have a poultry industry, a dairy or a cattle industry in British Columbia. If we do have an industry it will be such a small one it will be unable to look after the needs of the area. As I see it then, Mr. Speaker, we in British Columbia find ourselves in the
1034	HOUSE OF
Canadian Wheat Board Act unfortunate position of looking to the future with declining poultry, dairy and cattle industries because of the sale of these cheap grains between wheat farmers and livestock and poultry producers on the prairies. When that time arrives the wheat farmer who did require this cash, about which we hear so often in this house, is going to be in the position of being able to sell his wheat to the wheat board. Then the poultry producer on the prairies will be out of business, as will the cattle producer.
This can mean only one thing, Mr. Speaker. Before this act is extended for an indefinite stage-certainly it will pass this house, because we are all in support of it-the Minister of Trade and Commerce should set up a factfinding board to discover what effect it is going to have on the economy of the country as a whole. As I see it today we have a form of interprovincial dumping. It is not dumping in the true sense of goods being dumped from one country into another, but rather from a neighbouring province such as Alberta into British Columbia or possibly from Manitoba into Ontario. I am satisfied that the minister should have an examination made of this whole matter in the near future.
Now, once costs to the prairie farmer producing cattle and livestock go up to the degree I spoke of earlier, then he is going out of the poultry and livestock business. When he has ready cash he will do as he always has; he will become a grain farmer again. When he is in that position he is going to have to charge exactly the same price to the British Columbia producer. Then these poultry or livestock products, whatever they may be, will be shipped from the prairie provinces across the mountains, and we in British Columbia will have to pay the additional cost of refrigeration, the higher freight for carrying this type of product, and the handling charges which are considerably more than the handling charges for grain.
I indicated earlier that I believe in orderly marketing. I believe in this wheat board act. However, the British Columbia producer, who believes also in orderly marketing, is asking this question. Why is it not possible for the British Columbia poultry or livestock producer to get from his prairie counterpart, from the grain producers on the prairies, grain at the same price the prairie wheat farmer charges his neighbour, especially when these grains are going to be fed to animals? The fact is that it would be quite simple to give the primary producer in British Columbia or in Ontario a book the same as the grain farmer on the prairies has. It would be very easy to establish what 

he was doing with that grain. The act could provide for heavy penalties for misuse of the grain. It would not have to be sold by one producer to another, but it would make it possible for primary producers to get wheat and would give agriculture as a whole a lift, not only on the prairies but also in my own region.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would request-and I am quite sincere in this- that the minister discuss this matter with the government. Then the government could take the initiative and immediately set up a fact-finding board to determine:
(a)	The immediate effect on the poultry, dairy and livestock industries in British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces, depending upon feed grains from those areas subject to the continuation of the wheat board act;
(b)	The long-term effect of continuation of this act in these same areas.
Further, I would request that the government take the initiative in immediately setting up this fact-finding board to determine the effect of a short-term or long-term continuation of the act in both heavy and light crop years on the prairies, and upon consumer prices in those provinces not directly affected by the wheat board legislation, that is provinces such as British Columbia or Ontario.
Finally, I would ask that the fact-finding board bring in a report to parliament at the earliest possible time with such recommendations as they might make with respect to modifications to the act as a result of their findings. I contend most seriously that the bread basket of Canada should be the boon and not the bane of the agriculture industries which are dependent upon it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take a few minutes to discuss this bill which is now before the house, a bill which appears periodically to renew the compulsory powers of the Canadian wheat board. Before commencing my remarks I should like to say I am sorry the Leader of the Opposition is not in his seat. This is not a criticism, because I fully appreciate the tremendous task that lies ahead of him and I appreciate that he must have great demands on his time. However, this is the first opportunity I have had of addressing the house since he assumed the leadership of his party and became leader of the official opposition in this house.
I did want to say to him that I was very pleased when he took over the leadership of the party, and I wish him a long stay in opposition. As a matter of fact I intend to

deal this afternoon mostly with the remarks he made in opening this discussion, and I shall make my contribution toward keeping him in opposition as long as I can.
In opening the discussion on this bill the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave a full review of the history and the early development of the Canadian wheat board. It is a good thing to have this information placed on the records of this house from time to time, because nobody can actually appreciate or fully understand the present set-up of the wheat board without knowing the early beginnings and the various stages of development through which it went.
After the Minister of Trade and Commerce was through the Leader of the Opposition thought he would add to what had been said, and he proceeded to put a new interpretation *-an interpretation which I thought was fantastic-on what actually happened in 1935 when the Canadian Wheat Board Act was enacted. In other words, he attempted to put the blame for the failure of the Tories in 1935 on the Liberal opposition of the day. I am fully aware that the Liberals in 1935 were a very formidable opposition. As a matter of fact they chased the government out of office and practically ran them out of the country; certainly they chased them out of the west, and they have never recovered since. But to suggest that the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, in the last few days of the session, held, as the Leader of the Opposition said, some discussions with the opposition as to what type of legislation he would bring in just before the election is to my mind rather fantastic, because actually that is not exactly what happened.
The whole record of what took place in 1935 is available for anybody to see. The question that arises is why would the Conservative government actually enact any legislation at all in 1935 if they did not believe in it? The truth of the matter is that in 1935 the Tories had no sympathy with the compulsory board in the first place, and they tried, apparently as they are trying now, to put the blame for their failure on the opposition. The fact of the matter is that the legislation was referred to a select committee of the house, and it was the government itself that demanded its own bill in the committee before it was reported back. Therefore, actually the Liberal opposition never had a chance to vote against the bill in the first place.
The opposition in 1935 were too smart to pull any chestnuts out of the fire for their Tory opponents. They left in the bill a great many sections that would have made the Canadian wheat board a complete monopoly 82715-661	!
Canadian Wheat Board Act as far as the movement and transportation of grain was concerned. I believe the sections of the act were sections 9, 10, 11 and 16. These sections would have made a completely compulsory board, but when the Conservative government proclaimed the act they very carefully left out all those sections and they were never proclaimed by the government. Actually they could not have been very determined to have a compulsory board in those days.
This has been the official policy of the Conservative party from 1935 right up to the present day, as far as I know. The last time this matter was fully debated at a Conservative convention was in 1948. I think a great many people in this country remember what happened at the 1948 convention. That was when the Free Press referred to this particular phase of the convention as the "doubletalk division". There was quite a row; the funny cat of the wheat board was let out of the bag and the famous resolution of the 1948 convention ended up in this way:
"We favour a return to the wheat board; that the wheat board of 1935 be revived in respect to those farmers who wish to sell their wheat to the wheat board"; but they add these words: "by any other means".
And then they had a long discussion as to whether it should be "any other means, alternative market or straight open market"; but that was the official Conservative policy up until the last convention. Of course I do not claim to know what took place there, but I have not seen or heard of any new resolution to take precedence over the last one.
In 1943 and 1949 the previous leader, Hon. George Drew, took the exact position that the Conservatives took in 1935. I have here just for the record a report of the speech of the then leader of the opposition in 1949, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen. He spoke at Melfort, Saskatchewan, on May 25, 1949, and I quote:	1	1 I
Outlining his party's agricultural policy at a Victoria day rally in this prairie town, Mr. Drew said the Progressive Conservatives believed the Candian wheat board, now the sole marketing agency for wheat, should revert to the 1935 status.
As I say, so far as I know, this has been pretty well the official policy of the Conservative party all the way down from 1935 to this day. I do not know whether any change was made at the last convention, but we shall probably hear about that during this debate or at a later date during the year.
The other day, while another member was speaking, the hon. member for Brant-Haldi-mand (Mr. Charlton) interjected what he thought to be the stand of his party on the Canadian wheat board. He interjected that if anybody wanted to know what their stand

Canadian Wheat Board Act was all he had to do was to read the speech of the Leader of the Opposition at the opening of this discussion.
