The Leader of the Opposition proceeded to say again at page 893 of Hansard that he is for the Canadian wheat board. He said that during the operation of the Canada-United Kingdom wheat agreement-mind you, this is a five-year period-"the wheat board did not operate for the benefit of the western farmer". A little later on he went on to point out that the board was operating for political considerations in 1949, and that it was operating for political considerations in 1953. I would take it that by the same token the board must be operating under political dictation this year, because again this year it is making an interim payment, and there is likely to be an election this year as there was in the other years mentioned. Therefore, if it did not operate for the benefit of the producer from 1945 to 1949 and did not operate for the benefit of the farmer in 1949, 1953 and 1956, one would ask the obvious question. When did it operate to the advantage of the producer? That kind of support for the Canadian wheat board is hardly a declaration of faith in its operation.
I am afraid the official opposition have been doing this, not only now but in the past.
I think at the last session the present Leader of the Opposition was one of those who advocated very strenuously that a committee of businessmen be appointed as salesmen to be sent throughout the world to find more markets for our grain.
In effect that is simply to say that they want to take the sale of grain out of the hands of the Canadian wheat board.
Nothing of the sort; it was to get markets, not to deal with grain.

If the bulk of the responsibility for selling the grain is given to another body it is certainly not an indication in any man's language of faith in the ability of the board to sell grain. All in all there are too many people in this country and particularly in this house who constantly pay lip service to the organization and then proceed to criticize, damage and condemn its operations. Surely if the operations are not successful and are not working to the advantage of the farmer the organization cannot be a good one. There is no point in paying lip service to the organization unless you are ready to give it your support. I can understand certain criticisms being made, but when you criticize the very


essence of the operations of the board then it is a much more serious matter. This business of accusing the board of playing politics simply because it happened to make an interim payment during an election year is just plain nonsense.
I might remind the Leader of the Opposition that there was a member of his party who tried that several years ago. He was the first one to bring criticism of that nature into this house. That hon. member never came back after he made his criticism, and he heard a great deal about it in his own constituency. I am quite sure the producer would justifiably resent any criticism of that type. The argument that the board is playing politics because it borrows money to make a payment to the farmer-
Just before an election.

-does not hold water. It reveals that those who make that charge do not understand the operations of the board. The Canadian wheat board could never make a payment of any kind if they did not borrow. We started this year with a surplus of close to 500 million bushels of wheat, and if we have a crop similar to last year's we will be faced with a surplus of approximately one billion bushels. Even with an average crop it takes approximately three or four years to dispose of a surplus of that kind, and if you have a series of crops which are greater than average, such as we have had during the last three or four years, then the surplus cannot be disposed of in a period of under six or seven years at best. At that rate the producer would have to wait a long time before he could receive any payment. Of course it is untenable to argue that because the farmer received an interim payment it is an effort on the part of the government to obtain votes.
In the first place there is not a single farmer in western Canada who does not realize that when an interim payment is made it is money from the sale of his own grain. It is ridiculous to suggest that you can influence the farmer by telling him that the wheat board is making a payment. The farmer knows very well that the money does not come from the government or the treasury. He is fully aware that the money comes from the wheat board, and the farmer makes a big distinction between the Canadian wheat board and the Canadian government. The farmer has more sense than to believe that the money comes from the government. It has been the practice over the years to endeavour to space payments periodically as conditions warrant them. Surely we are not going to argue that because an election is pending the wheat board should withhold any payment to the

farmer. Anyone who suggests that the payment which has just been announced is for election purposes will be laughed out of the west.
Mention has been made of the United Kingdom wheat agreement. In dealing with this subject the Leader of the Opposition, as he has on many occasions in the past, attempted to leave the impression that this was entirely the responsibility of the government and that he and his party had not supported this agreement. He was very careful to time his remarks and to couch them in language to suit his convenience. He proceeded to decry the great losses under the United Kingdom agreement and concluded by saying, as I recall his words, "However, the contract was entered into".
The hon. member should have said that the contract was entered into in the first place and the Conservative party at that time supported the United Kingdom agreement. I remember it as if it were yesterday. For the benefit of those who were not here at the time I will place on the record the words of the leader of the official opposition of the day, Mr. John Bracken; and I quote from page 4811 of Hansard for August 14, 1946:
I rise at this time to criticize the government's wheat policy. But before doing so, let me say this, with respect to the United Kingdom wheat agreement. Any agreement such as this which tends to level out the inequalities, and the wide fluctuations of prices in the past, is a step in the right direction. Even this agreement is better than no agreement at all . . .
He then goes on to give some of his reasons for supporting the agreement. No one in the official opposition should now criticize the agreement. Every word of criticism spoken by the Leader of the Opposition rings false, because the agreement was passed unanimously with no dissenting vote at the time of its adoption.
While I am dealing with the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition I might say I was rather amazed at the way he treated the question of the United States fire-sale policy, or rather the policy of selling grain at cut-rate prices. He intimated that the Canadian government was not aggressive enough in dealing with our friends to the south. I think we all appreciate that the policy of the United States creates a very real problem under which it is difficult for our agency the Canadian wheat board to sell grain in the world markets. No one wants to make it any worse than it is. I would like to quote the contention of the Leader of the Opposition when he spoke in this debate on February 1, 1957, as reported at page 895 of Hansard:
Canadian Wheat Board Act
We supply the United States with a major portion of its needs to forge the shield of freedom. We are a have country and they are becoming a have-not country.
With all due reference I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that while perhaps the United States is becoming a have-not country, it is a long way from having reached that stage, and if anyone went to Washington today with that opinion in mind he would receive quite a surprise because they are still an extremely powerful country. The attitude expressed by the present Leader of the Opposition reflects perfectly the attitude of one of his ablest predecessors, who attempted to express an attitude of that kind in the thirties with disastrous results about which we all know. To attempt at this time to revert to the attitude voiced in those days will accomplish no good results and may very well cause a great deal of harm. An attitude of co-operation is still best, and I am confident that eventually, once they have put their house in order, our friends to the south are going to appreciate our problems more and more and will cooperate with us fully. Then we will be able to meet the situation.
I would not want the impression to be left that because of the fire-sale policy of our friends to the south the Canadian wheat board has been losing markets over the years. There came to my hand just this afternoon the latest report of the Canadian wheat board for 1955-56. This contains a table giving Canada's percentage of the world wheat export market. Starting from the end of the war the United States have been the largest exporters of grain, except in 1952 and 1953. Actually we are in no worse position today than we were in the years since the end of the war. Of course we were once a great leader and exceeded the United States by a wide margin before the war, but as we all know the United States at that time were not making any efforts to grow wheat. It is only from the war on that wheat production has been increased.

Is that not a loss for 1954?

When you talk about a loss you have to take a comparison. You are using a comparison. If you take from 1945 to 1952 it will be seen that the United States had a greater share of the world market than we had. Then we recovered, and today they have only 4.4 per cent more than we have. Considering the conditions under which they operate, give-away sales and so on, I think it can be said that the Canadian wheat board has had a most successful operation and that the future is not as dark as some would have us believe. The picture is still a good one.
I have the figures for grain movements from August 1 to December 31 of last year. The clearings at the lakehead were 367 million bushels as compared with 267 million bushels the previous year. Deliveries at elevator points from the beginning of the crop year until January of this year were 251 million bushels as compared with 167 million bushels for the previous year. Exports were 187 million bushels as compared with 132 million bushels. In the case of wheat there was a 35 per cent increase; in the case of barley a 60 per cent increase. Those are the figures from the first of the crop year, August 1, 1956, to January of this year. If that trend continues this should be an outstanding year. If things should enter into the picture to cloud it there is still every indication that 1956-57 will be better than the previous year.
Would the hon. member put on the record the prices which the United States farmers received in those years as compared with the prices received by Canadian farmers, so we may make a comparison?

The hon. members from Saskatchewan are constantly criticizing and harping that they in that province are being treated unfairly. Actually all the figures disprove that contention, they are being misled as a result of following these quota figures only, figures which do not have the meaning that is given to them. The important thing is not how high a quota is but how much grain a farmer is allowed to deliver. That, after all, is what matters, and I say that on that basis there is no complaint to come from Saskatchewan members; they have had their share, and a full share.
Can the hon. member state an instance when a Saskatchewan member has complained that the Manitoba quotas are too high?

Since you mention it, I certainly will. I have not an instance before me at this moment, but Hansard was cluttered up last session with examples. I will not say that the hon. member himself did not do it; certainly the hon. member for Assiniboia did, because that prompted me to get up and refer to this matter during last session. I certainly will look this up and give hon. members many instances of it. What
Canadian Wheat Board Act they did was point to the quota in Manitoba in relation to the average quota in Saskatchewan, and they did it on more than one occasion.
I am taking exception to that, because it was misleading. It is not a proper basis for comparison. The proper basis is, as I have said, the amount of grain the farmer is allowed to deliver. That is the real consideration, and that is the one which the board should consider above everything else.

Should we adjourn the debate, Mr. Speaker?
I understand that hon. members must go to the other place at a quarter to six.

speechtext: The proceedings are automatically interrupted by the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod whenever the knock is heard. In the meantime, if the hon. member wishes to continue the debate he may do so. If no hon. member wishes to speak we can, of course, sit and wait.

Mr. Speaker, the other day the hon. member for Assiniboia pointed out that members of this party would vote for the second reading of this bill, which is to extend the life of the Canadian wheat board for another five years. Members of this party support the Canadian Wheat Board Act; as a matter of fact we would like to see the legislation made permanent, because we believe western farmers have so much to gain from the orderly marketing of their wheat. Indeed, we feel rather sorry that the government did not see fit to bring in legislation making this permanent in order to show the confidence they had in this type of marketing.
I would like, second, to point out that members of this group have indicated from time to time that we would like to see the Canadian wheat board handle other grain besides wheat, oats and barley, which are presently under its control. I feel, sir, that the Canadian wheat board has proved the kind of organization which western farmers have been demanding over the years. Those of us who have farmed in the west, and who represent farming constituencies, will remember the years prior to the operation of the Canadian wheat board when western farmers were at the mercy of the Winnipeg grain exchange. I can recall that each year, after the crop was seeded, reports would come out that there was a big crop in the making in western Canada. Away fell the prices that wheat would bring. As soon as the grain was ready to move to the elevators, wheat prices went down. That is why so much has been done over the years by organized farmers to try to find some method

by which they can sell their grain without speculation on the Winnipeg grain exchange.
Throughout the years the C.C.F. has advocated this type of orderly marketing.
